item.title: Tear gas, sound grenades disperse Gazipur workers; traffic resumes
item.description:
Traffic on the Dhaka-Tangail highway returned to normal on Saturday after law enforcement personnel dispersed protesting garment workers in Gazipur's Kaliakair using tear gas and sound grenades, ending a blockade that disrupted traffic for around one and a half hours.
The workers had blocked the highway in the Palli Bidyut area, demanding a wage increase. The protest began at around 9:30am, with normal traffic resuming by 11am.
Mohammad Amjad Hossain, superintendent of Gazipur Industrial Police, confirmed the development.
According to witnesses, workers at several garment factories in and around the Palli Bidyut area did not report for their shifts on Saturday. Instead, they began protesting inside their respective factories before moving onto the highway and blocking it, triggering severe traffic congestion.
Following reports of the blockade, members of the Industrial Police, district police and Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) arrived at the scene. They used tear gas and sound grenades to disperse the protesters, allowing traffic to resume.
Mohammad Jasim Uddin, superintendent of Gazipur District Police, said blockades had been reported at several points along the Dhaka-Tangail highway on Saturday morning.
The protesters were later dispersed using sound grenades, he said, adding that traffic along the Chandra-Konabari stretch had returned to normal.
Earlier on Saturday, workers from six to seven garment factories in the Palli Bidyut area had taken to the highway, bringing traffic to a halt. Industrial Police and district police personnel intervened, while law enforcement agencies remained on high alert.

item.title: Minimum Wage Board for garment workers to meet on Nov 16
item.description:
The Minimum Wage Board, formed to recommend minimum wage rates for workers and employees of all categories in the garment industry, will hold its third meeting on November 16.
The meeting will begin at 11am at the Department of Labour on the 19th floor of the Shrom Bhaban in Bijoynagar, Dhaka.
Board Chairman Syed Azad Subhani, a District and Sessions Judge, will preside over the meeting, convened under Section 139 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006.
According to a notice issued by the board, the first agenda of the meeting will be the submission of a written proposal on minimum wage rates by the representative of the garment industry owners.
The meeting will also discuss formulating recommendations on minimum wage rates for workers and employees across all categories in the garment sector.

item.title: Fifth shipment of uranium arrives at Rooppur plant
item.description:
The fifth shipment of uranium fuel for the second unit of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Pabna arrived at the project site early Saturday, marking another step towards the plant's commissioning.
The fuel, sourced from Russia, was transported to the plant in three specialised lorries at around 5:30am under tight security.
Members of the Bangladesh Army and other law enforcement agencies provided security during the transportation.
According to project sources, six shipments of uranium fuel have reached the site so far: one for the first unit and five for the second unit.
Under the delivery plan drawn up by Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom, 163 uranium fuel assemblies are scheduled to be delivered for the second unit through seven cargo flights. Another 48 assemblies are planned to arrive in two separate cargo shipments as reserve fuel for the first unit. This will bring the total number of shipments to nine.
Meanwhile, preparations for commissioning the plant's first unit are also underway. The unit is currently in the "Power Start-up Stage-C" phase, for which the Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) Chairman granted approval on October 29.
During this phase, the reactor's power output will be gradually increased to test the performance of various plant components, including turbines, generators and safety systems.
Once the tests are completed successfully, the generator of the first unit will be connected to the national power grid in a process known as synchronization.
According to the project plan, the first unit is expected to supply around 300 megawatts of electricity to the national grid on a trial basis in November. However, the start of trial power generation will depend on the completion of the necessary tests and approval from the regulatory authority.
Built with Russian technology, the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant comprises two units equipped with VVER-1200 reactors. Once fully operational, the plant is expected to significantly boost the country's power generation capacity and strengthen long-term energy security.

Climate pledges fall short as Bangladesh seeks $11bn annually
item.description:
Bangladesh has urged developed countries to accelerate climate finance delivery, saying it needs between $10 billion and $11 billion annually to address the impacts of climate change, as international funding commitments continue to fall short of the needs of vulnerable nations.
The country is already spending an estimated $4.5 billion to $5 billion annually from domestic sources on climate-related initiatives, highlighting the scale of investment required to strengthen resilience and support its transition to a lower-carbon economy.
The demand was raised at a press briefing by the Bangladesh delegation on Thursday during the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, where climate finance remains a central issue in negotiations between developed and developing countries.
Environment, Forest and Climate Change Minister Abdul Awal Mintoo said the progress made in pledging climate finance had not been matched by the actual delivery of funds.
The delegation called for more accessible international financing, particularly grant-based support, arguing that complex approval procedures and delays in disbursement were preventing vulnerable countries from responding effectively to climate risks.
Foreign Affairs State Minister Shama Obaed Islam stressed that financial assistance must reach communities facing the greatest climate threats rather than remain tied up in lengthy funding processes.
Responding to a question from Carbon Brief about Bangladesh's expectations from the climate finance work programme, a delegation representative said greater clarity was needed on funding responsibilities and distribution mechanisms.
The representative also highlighted the challenges facing communities displaced by river erosion, underscoring the need for financing arrangements that can respond to the immediate needs of climate-affected populations.
Bangladesh's demands reflect broader concerns among least developed countries (LDCs) over the widening gap between climate finance commitments and the resources available to implement adaptation measures.
In its written statement, the delegation backed the LDC Group's call for a threefold increase in adaptation finance to $120 billion annually before 2035.
It urged developed countries to meet their existing climate finance commitments and expand grant-based assistance, particularly to support the implementation of National Adaptation Plans in climate-vulnerable countries.
Bangladesh also called for simplified and more direct access to the Green Climate Fund, the Global Environment Facility and the Adaptation Fund.
The delegation supported an LDC proposal to establish a platform connecting national adaptation priorities with potential funders and development partners, aiming to bridge the gap between countries' climate plans and their implementation.
On the Global Goal on Adaptation, Bangladesh said the proposed Belém Adaptation Indicators should provide a meaningful way to measure progress in climate resilience without introducing additional reporting requirements for developing countries.
It also called for greater financial and technical support for locally led adaptation, recognising the importance of community-level initiatives in responding to climate impacts.
Bangladesh raised concerns over the limited resources available to the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, saying its existing financing was insufficient to meet demand from submitted proposals.
The delegation called for increased financial contributions, simplified direct-access arrangements and faster disbursement to countries experiencing the consequences of climate change.
It also stressed that funding should address both economic losses, such as damage to infrastructure and livelihoods, and non-economic losses, including displacement and damage to cultural and social assets.
The written statement further said Bangladesh was among the first five countries expected to receive $30 million each from the Climate Investment Funds.
Coastal infrastructure and climate-resilient agriculture were identified as priority areas for the expected financing.
The delegation also raised concerns over unilateral climate-related trade measures, including the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).
It warned that such measures could place additional pressure on businesses, workers and exporters in developing countries, potentially undermining their economic development efforts.
Responding to questions about whether the issue should feature in a COP31 decision, a delegation representative argued that countries that had benefited from activities contributing to the climate crisis should also take responsibility for supporting those most affected.
The representative said climate policies should not create additional trade barriers for developing economies already facing the costs of climate impacts and the transition to cleaner production.
Journalists also questioned whether COP negotiations included dedicated financing to protect children and safeguard their education in climate-vulnerable countries.
A delegation representative said they were not aware of any specific financing demand exclusively dedicated to children, while referring to ongoing efforts to strengthen healthcare services.
On the broader question of benefits for vulnerable communities, the delegation said international negotiations had helped establish climate change as a shared global challenge and encouraged countries to develop action plans, although implementation remained a major challenge.
Bangladesh accounts for less than 0.5% of global greenhouse gas emissions but has reaffirmed its commitment to reducing emissions under its updated Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC).
The country has pledged to reduce emissions by 6.39% below its business-as-usual projection by 2035 using domestic efforts, with a further 13.92% reduction conditional on receiving international support.
The delegation backed extending the Mitigation Work Programme through 2030, calling for sector-specific action supported by adequate financing, technology transfer and capacity-building.
It also stressed that the transition to a low-carbon economy must be just and inclusive, prioritising least developed and other climate-vulnerable countries while protecting employment, expanding skills development and providing social protection for affected workers and communities.
Bangladesh said it would continue coordinating with the LDC Group, the G77 and China, and other international partners during the second week of COP31 to push for stronger outcomes on climate finance.
For Dhaka, the central challenge is no longer simply securing new financial pledges but ensuring that promised resources reach countries and communities facing the consequences of a crisis they have contributed relatively little to creating.
This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership, a journalism fellowship organised by Internews' Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

item.title: 34 BGB platoons deployed in Dhaka, Gazipur, Narayanganj
item.description:
A total of 34 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) have been deployed across key industrial areas in Dhaka, Gazipur and Narayanganj on Saturday to maintain law and order, ensure security and prevent any untoward incidents.
The BGB personnel have been deployed in several strategic locations, including Savar, Ashulia, Hemayetpur, Jirani and Jamgara in Dhaka district; Shibu Market, Katherpul, Jalkuri, BSCIC Industrial Estate, Chashara, Kanchpur and Shimrail in Narayanganj; and Chandra, Palli Bidyut, Mouchak, Ambag Kata, Bhogra Bypass, Gacha, Salna, Naojor and Kashimpur in Gazipur.
The deployed personnel are working in coordination with the local administration and other law enforcement agencies and remain on high alert to respond to any emerging situation.
Meanwhile, BGB headquarters has activated a monitoring cell to oversee the situation and coordinate field-level operations through technology-based surveillance.
The monitoring system uses drones and body-worn cameras, alongside live footage transmitted from various devices, to facilitate continuous surveillance and monitor developments in the field.

item.title: Dhaka ranks world's third most polluted city Saturday morning
item.description:
Dhaka, the densely populated capital of Bangladesh, ranked third among the world’s most polluted cities on Saturday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 195 at 9:14am.
The city’s air was classified as "unhealthy", indicating a health threat, according to the AQI report.
India’s Delhi, Pakistan’s Lahore and India’s Kolkata occupied the first, second, and fourth spots on the list, with AQI scores of 235, 232, and 192, respectively.
According to the AQI scale, a reading between 50 and 100 is considered "moderate", with generally acceptable air quality, though sensitive individuals should limit prolonged outdoor exertion. AQI levels of 101–150 are "unhealthy for sensitive groups", 151–200 is "unhealthy", 201–300 is "very unhealthy", and readings above 301 are considered "hazardous", posing severe health risks.
The AQI, which reports daily air quality, informs residents how clean or polluted the air is and highlights potential health effects. In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five key pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution. Air quality usually deteriorates in winter and improves during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that air pollution causes about seven million deaths worldwide each year, primarily from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, and acute respiratory infections.

Proteas eager to continue WTC momentum against Bangladesh
item.description:
Having jumped to the second spot in the ICC World Test Championship Rankings, South Africa will now face Bangladesh in the ongoing cycle.
Despite the visitors being ranked lower in the WTC Standings than their previous opponents - Australia - the hosts will be determined to not let their feet off the accelerator as they look to make a push for next year's WTC Final.
"In international cricket, you can't take any series for granted," Kagiso Rabada told the reporters ahead of the two-match series.
"There are always high stakes on ⁠every game that you play. And moving into this series against Bangladesh, they'll be heightened in their spirits, looking at the way they've played in recent times.
"It's actually exciting, you know? You want to be up against the best opposition that you can be.
"And I think they'd want to come here and prove a point and I'm really looking forward to this battle. I think ‌it ⁠will show how healthy cricket is."
Bangladesh are currently fifth in the WTC Standings, and are coming on the back of a 1-0 series defeat at the hands of the West Indies.
Previously, the team had registered a well-earned draw in a two-match series in Australia. A performance that hasn't gone unnoticed in the Proteas camp.
For the reigning ICC World Test Championship winners, the upcoming series is also about ensuring they continue to vie for the top two spot in the Standings.
"I think it's human nature, we've found ourselves on that side before where ⁠we probably got a bit too complacent," he said.
"It's something that we have to guard against, to really give it our best shot and not drop the intensity, to keep our standards right ⁠up there.
"We're not really thinking about the result, we're just going to think about how we want to play, because that's what we've been doing these past two years, ⁠having that desperation to win.
"And yeah, getting into the faces of our opponents, that's exactly how we want to play. We'll be looking to do more of the same," he added.

item.title: Stench of 'Sandpapergate' set to linger as scandal reignites
item.description:
Australian captain Pat Cummins wants to draw a line under "Sandpapergate" and move on, but the stench of the 2018 ball-tampering scandal is set to linger after a week of sensational accusations and denials.
Cummins held an intense 70-minute press conference on Friday and answered every question thrown at him after former teammate Usman Khawaja reopened old wounds with the release of his explosive autobiography.
In the book, he claimed the whole team, including Cummins, knew about the plot to alter the ball with sandpaper during the Cape Town Test against South Africa.
Only David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft were held responsible by Cricket Australia for the incident that shattered the nation's reputation, with all three sent home in disgrace and banned.
Cummins repeated multiple times that he was not aware of the plan, insisting Khawaja's version of events was "100 percent wrong".
"I don't want to talk about this again after today ... because at some point we've got to move on," he added.
His plea drew support from Justin Langer, who took over as head coach when Darren Lehmann quit in the wake of the scandal.
"Hopefully, that will put some sort of line in the sand because we have to move on," Langer told SEN radio.
"There's too many people being hurt in Australian cricket ... and that includes the Australian public.
"When I talk about Australian cricket, it's about the public, it's about the fans, it's about the players, it's about everyone who's involved: the past players, the present players, future players. We have to draw a line in the sand somewhere."
Another former Test great Greg Chappell also urged an end to the in-fighting.
"We don't want to see Australian cricket eating itself and having a little spat within the family," he told reporters.
"Hopefully Pat's put a bit of a line under it and we can start getting on with the summer of cricket."
While calls to put the issue to bed mount, it could blow up again with several key players yet to comment, notably Smith and Bancroft, while Khawaja has media commitments to sell his book.
Warner, who has strongly backed close friend Khawaja's new version of events, made clear he will not rest "until the truth is out there".
- Pick your side -
"The biggest error of the Cummins Q and A was his belief that his appearance would allow everyone to draw a line under the affair and move on," national broadcaster ABC said in an analysis.
"That's not happening. We're dealing with hurt feelings here, fractured relationships and bruised egos and nebulous concepts of truth and justice.
"You better pick your side, if you haven't already, because this is never going away."
Whether what really happened is ever properly established remains to be seen with Cricket Australia adamant it will not be re-opening its investigation.
But the bonds of a 15-year friendship between Cummins, Khawaja and Warner have splintered.
Cummins accused Khawaja of being "flippant and casual" by dropping his bombshell claims eight years after the fact, suggesting some of them were "probably defamatory".
That prompted Warner to blast Cummins for throwing Khawaja "under the bus" and The Australian newspaper to declare that "a generation of Australian players is officially at war".
Cummins insists unity within the current Australian team, which includes Smith, remains strong despite the week's firestorm as they prepare for a home Test series against New Zealand in December-January.
He said he had spoken to Smith, who lost the captaincy and was banned for a year over "Sandpapergate", and suggested the veteran batsman was keen not to regurgitate the past.
"I have spoken to Smithy. Without breaking confidence, he is done with this, he wants to move on," said Cummins.
"This was very traumatic for him. If standing up today and answering all your questions helps everyone move on, then maybe it's a good thing."

item.title: Tearful Pochettino admits Man Utd move is one of his toughest decisions
item.description:
Mauricio Pochettino said Friday that leaving his role as USA boss to take charge of Manchester United was "one of the most difficult" decisions of his career as he prepares for one of football's toughest jobs.
The 54-year-old Argentine fought back tears as he bade an emotional farewell to US football, hours after the Premier League giants announced he would replace the sacked Michael Carrick.
The former Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea boss will take up his new position on November 18, with a monumental task ahead of him.
United have made their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years and are languishing in the Premier League relegation zone during the current international break.
Pochettino is understood to have signed a two-and-a-half-year deal at Old Trafford, taking him through to the end of the 2028/29 season.
"We learned a lot from you all, from this amazing country," Pochettino told a media conference in Fayetteville, Georgia. "I think this was one of the most difficult decisions of (my) career."
Pochettino, who led the USA to the last 16 at this year's World Cup, will oversee back-to-back CONCACAF Nations League matches against Haiti on Saturday and next Tuesday before leaving for England.
He said he had not considered a possible return to the Premier League when he signed a contract extension with US Soccer in August, but added the opportunity to join United was too good to turn down.
"I never said I wanted to go back in the Premier League," he said. "Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives."
US Soccer CEO and secretary general JT Batson said Pochettino had left a lasting legacy through his "leadership, professionalism and commitment to our players and culture".
The federation is reportedly set to receive around $10 million in compensation, plus more to cover the departure of Pochettino's coaching staff.
United said in a statement that Pochettino was "renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players".
"Pochettino has consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues," the club added.
The 20-time English champions are one of the giants of world football but have largely been also-rans since Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.
Pochettino is the eighth permanent manager tasked with returning the Red Devils to former glories.
He started his Premier League managerial career with Southampton before joining Tottenham, where he never finished lower than fifth during his five full seasons in charge and also reached the 2019 Champions League final.
Pochettino claimed the first trophies of his managerial career with PSG, collecting the 2021 French Cup and 2022 Ligue 1 title, but did not see out his contract in Paris.
He returned to the dugout at Chelsea in 2023 but only lasted one season.
The former Argentina defender, who has been linked with the United job on several previous occasions, faces a baptism of fire at the home of fierce rivals Liverpool on November 22.
He must unite a club that is deeply divided on and off the pitch.
United captain Bruno Fernandes was dropped last month after he criticised Carrick's tactics and Lisandro Martinez took a public swipe at the United hierarchy over a lack of investment.
Angry fans vented their frustration at the club's ownership following the sacking of the popular Carrick, who won multiple trophies as a player.
Despite fierce and persistent protests over two decades, the US-based Glazer family still hold a majority stake in United, which Malcolm Glazer bought via a leveraged takeover in 2005, saddling the club with huge debts.
Any hopes the arrival of British billionaire Jim Ratcliffe as a minority owner in 2024 would signal a new dawn have since faded.
Carrick issued an emotional statement Friday wishing United "nothing but success", adding that his love for the club "never dies".

item.title: Bangladesh face Pakistan in crucial SAFF semifinal today
item.description:
Bangladesh will look to move one step closer to ending their 23 years wait for a second SAFF Championship title when they lock-horn Pakistan in a crucial semifinal at the National Stadium here on Saturday.
The match kicks off at 8:30 pm and will be televised live by private satellite channel T Sports. Defending champions India will face Bhutan in the first semifinal at 3 pm on the same day.
The hosts headed into the knockout clash full of confidence after topping Group A with a perfect record, winning both their matches without conceding a goal.
The hosts promised an exciting contest as they look to turn their impressive group-stage performance into a place in the title-deciding match.
The boys in red and green started their tournament campaign with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Bhutan before earning an overwhelming 4-0 victory over Sri Lanka in their final group match.
Thanks to Shamit Shome, Hamza Choudhury, Farhaan Ali Wahid and Rakib Hossain who were on target against Sri Lanka, demonstrating Bangladesh's attacking strength and growing confidence.
Earlier, Bangladesh midfielder Jamal Bhuyan already acknowledged the threat posed by Pakistan, saying the team has shifted their focus to the semifinal following their convincing win over Sri Lanka.
The hosts, however, have some injury concerns in their defensive department. Right-back Saad Uddin has been ruled out of the remainder of the tournament after sustaining an Achilles tendon injury against Sri Lanka.
The availability and fitness of other defenders will also be important for the coaching staff ahead of the crucial encounter.
Bangladesh will also get the home ground advantage as they will get bounty support from their passionate football fans.
Hamza and Co. seek to reach the final in front of their supporters.
A victory would take Bangladesh one step closer to ending their long wait for regional football glory.
The challenges are particularly high for Bangladesh, who are chasing their second SAFF Championship title after lifting the trophy for the first back in 2003 in home ground. The boys in red and green have been waiting for 23 years to reclaim the regional crown.
With a place in the final at stake, Bangladesh will need to maintain their attacking momentum against a determined Pakistan side.
However, Pakistan are also expected to provide a much tougher challenge in the semifinal against Bangladesh.
Pakistan began their campaign with a fighting 3-2 goals defeat to India in their opening group match before bounced back to register a convincing 3-0 goals win over Maldives in their final group match.

item.title: Silva says Portugal ready for spotlight without Ronaldo
item.description:
Portugal midfielder Bernardo Silva said Friday his team could cope with any extra pressure on them following Cristiano Ronaldo's international retirement, ahead of their first match without the superstar forward.
Jorge Jesus's side host Denmark in Braga on Saturday in the Nations League, with a tribute planned for their all-time leading goalscorer.
Real Madrid's Silva, who inherits the captain's armband from Ronaldo, admitted that the striker had been the main focus for much of the past two decades but backed the team to cope with the pressure in the 41-year-old's absence.
"Everyone knows the weight Cristiano carries. Most people went to the stadium to see Cristiano, many went just for him, and that's not going to happen now," Silva told reporters.
"The national team players are used to the spotlight, the pressure, and the responsibility, as well as being pointed at when things don't go well -- so that's not an issue."
Portugal will pay tribute to five-time Ballon d'Or winner Ronaldo before the game against Denmark, with media reporting the squad will walk out wearing number seven jerseys, Ronaldo's number.
Whether Ronaldo will be present is unknown, after he fell out with veteran coach Jorge Jesus in September.
Last week Ronaldo said he was bringing down the curtain on his storied international career.
Ronaldo made his debut for Portugal in 2003 and went on to play a world record 234 times for his country, scoring 146 goals.
"Nobody can forget Cris's 23 years in the national team and everything he did," Jesus told reporters.
"I think (paying tribute) is a brilliant idea to continue to remind us that he is a legend of Portuguese football."
Portugal have already sealed qualification to the quarter-finals of the Nations League, winning all four matches in Group A4.

item.title: Argentina beaten by Uruguay in first game since Messi retirement
item.description:
Argentina suffered a 2-1 defeat against Uruguay on Friday in their first game since Lionel Messi's retirement from international football.
A second-half own goal by Argentina defender Leonardo Balerdi followed by a fluky effort from Uruguay midfielder Maxi Araujo sealed defeat for the 2026 World Cup runners-up.
Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alavarez gave Argentina hope of a comeback with a 73rd-minute strike but Uruguay held on to clinch a third victory for new manager Diego Forlan.
Messi played his final game for Argentina in an emotional farewell friendly victory over Benin last month, calling time on a glittering career that spanned 207 caps and 125 goals.
With the 39-year-old genius missing, Argentina struggled to break down a resilient Uruguay team for long stretches of Friday's friendly.
Nico Paz had Argentina's best chance of the first half, but saw his shot well-saved by Uruguay goalkeeper Cristopher Fiermarin.
Uruguay made the breakthrough soon after half-time when a Giorgian de Arrascaeta free-kick from the left caused chaos in the Argentina defence.
Manchester United defender Lisandro Martinez attempted to clear with a header but his effort instead cannoned off team-mate Balerdi and into the net.
De Arrascaeta then set up Uruguay's second in the 53rd minute, his corner appearing to hit Araujo's shoulder before looping high into the net.
Alvarez pulled a goal back midway through the half, and had another good chance in stoppage time but Uruguay closed out the win.

item.title: The miracle cure in your Facebook feed is killing Bangladeshis
item.description:
Every Bangladeshi family knows the scene. My father is newly diagnosed with diabetes. The doctor's advice is the same as always: Medication, diet, regular monitoring, lifelong discipline. It is sound advice, and it is exhausting to follow.
Then his morning walk friend forwards a video to him. A man in a white coat promises a cure in seven days, with no injections and no side effects, for only Tk3,500 and cash on delivery.
This is not harmless chatter. It is a business, and its customers are dying.
Diabetes is a lifelong condition for which no cure currently exists. That inconvenient truth is the foundation of a thriving commercial ecosystem on Facebook and TikTok: Fake doctors, unregistered supplements, and "miracle" pills sold to people who are frightened, tired, or simply priced out of regular care.
Social media is filled with products claiming to replace insulin or conventional medication with herbal alternatives, despite no credible scientific evidence supporting those claims. Patients each month require hospitalization after following unqualified health advice found on social media and resulting in liver, kidney, or cardiovascular complications.
Think about what that number means. Families continue to pay for someone else's marketing copy with their organs. Now think about the patients who never made it to a hospital.
The word "herbal" does a great deal of the sellers' work. In a country with a long and respected tradition of traditional remedies, "natural" feels "safe." It is not.
A product with no declared dose, no tested purity, and no registration is simply an unknown substance. The danger is greatest when a patient stops a prescribed drug because a post told them they no longer need it.
What makes this scam distinctly Bangladeshi is how skilfully it borrows trust. Fraudsters know we respect the doctor, the professor, and the familiar newspaper masthead, so they counterfeit all three.
Dr Jahangir Kabir, a prominent health advocate who promotes lifestyle-based approaches to diabetes, has said dishonest groups are misusing his name to sell unregulated medicines.
He reports that hundreds of fake Facebook pages were created in his name, some even mimicking his verified profile's blue-badge image. A man who tells people to change how they eat and live found his face on the label of a bottle.
He is not alone. Microbiologist Dr Senjuti Saha discovered that her name and image were being used in a fraudulent campaign and filed a general diary at the police station.
Dismislab traced the "Optimax" diabetes product to counterfeit pages mimicking Prothom Alo, featuring fake interviews with "prominent" Bangladeshi professionals.
Even the health minister's identity has been hijacked: iIn 2024 the ministry had to warn that fake Facebook accounts were being opened in his name, with advertisements that could cheat the public.
When the scammer can wear the face of a trusted doctor and the logo of a trusted newspaper, "just don't believe everything online" is not advice. It is an abdication.
We have long assumed that more smartphones meant more awareness. The evidence is more troubling. Studies suggest that mobile phone ownership is associated with greater exposure to misinformation, not just greater access to information.
In a country where phones have reached the village before the specialist has, the same device that delivers a telemedicine consultation also delivers a "cure" for diabetes. In many cases, it is the second that arrives first.
Self-medication was already common long before Facebook. We buy tablets over the counter, trust a neighbour's prescription, and stretch a doctor's visit as far as it will go. Influencers did not create this habit. They have simply learned to monetize it.
Media professionals are not blameless. For years our response to health misinformation has been the occasional "myth-buster" column, published once, read by few, and forgotten by the next news cycle. The scammers publish daily. We cannot answer a daily campaign with an annual correction.
Newspapers need standing health fact-check desks, with trained reporters, a medical advisory panel, and the same institutional seriousness we give to political fact-checking. A fake diabetes ad should be treated with the same urgency as a fake political quote.
Television channels and online portals should produce short, shareable "spot the scam" segments in Bangla. Sixty seconds are enough to show a viewer how to check whether a doctor is registered with the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council, why "cure in seven days" is a warning rather than a promise, and why no pill replaces insulin. Content that is easy to forward to the family WhatsApp group is how we compete on the scammers' own ground.
We should use AI sensibly. Newsrooms can deploy language tools, including Bangla-capable ones, to flag viral health claims, repeated ad creatives, and suspicious pages at a scale no human desk can match.
But AI should only flag. Verification, context, and the final call must remain with trained editors and doctors. A machine can tell us where the fire is. It cannot tell us whether the person in the video is really a physician.
Finally, the media must stop accepting the framing that this is merely a "content moderation" problem. Content moderation means a platform deciding whether a post stays up.
What we are describing is the sale of unregistered medicinal products, under false identities, to sick people, for profit. That is consumer fraud and a public health offense.
The Directorate General of Drug Administration, the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission, the consumer rights authorities and law enforcement all have a role.
So do Meta and TikTok, which earn revenue from the very advertisements that deceive our citizens.
The press should keep asking the uncomfortable questions: Who approved this ad, who was paid, who was prosecuted, and how many times was it reported before it came down?
The next time a "miracle cure" appears in your feed, remember what it is: Someone's sales pitch, aimed at your parent's fear.
Insulin is not a conspiracy, and diabetes does not end in seven days. The sooner we say so, loudly, every single day, the fewer families will learn it in a hospital corridor.
Dewan Shahnoor Alam Sourav is a lecturer in the Department of Media Studies and Journalism at the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB). Can be reached at ds.alam.sourav@gmail.com .

item.title: How do I grieve someone I have not met yet?
item.description:
This is what I kept asking myself as I waited in the hospital, knowing that my 4.5-month pregnancy was coming to an end. Perhaps it is simply human nature to grow attached to the life growing inside you.
My entire life, I have catastrophized everything. The same happened when I found out I was pregnant. But I quickly tried to quiet that part of me and focus on doing my best.
Everything was going perfectly. I had no known risk factors, my scans had gone well, and my doctor had told me to schedule an appointment for the following month.
No one had warned me that even when everything seemed to be going well, it could all turn upside down in the blink of an eye.
I had gone to sleep when my amniotic fluid ruptured. Even half asleep, I knew what that meant. My pregnancy had ended. I was rushed to the hospital, and the duty doctor tried to console me: “We do not know yet.”
But I knew that the future I had already started imagining would no longer come to be.
I had to wait an excruciating 12 hours for my gynaecologist to examine me. She finally explained what would happen next. I would be given one dose of medication that day and more the following day to induce labour.
Miscarriage . Just one word, carrying a weight that is almost impossible to put into words. A grief so profound, yet one no one warns you about.
While I waited in the hospital for the procedures to be completed, my aunts, uncles, grandmothers, cousins, everyone, rallied around me. I was going through one of the most difficult periods of my life, but I was wrapped in a blanket of love.
The women around me told me their own stories of loss, their struggles, and how they had found a way through. Even though my own pain felt insurmountable, it was the strength I found in their stories that helped me through.
Despite medical science coming such a long way, no reason could be identified for why this was happening to me. The pregnancy was not advanced enough for there to be any hope of saving it, but it was also not early enough for my miscarriage to go unnoticed.
The medication I was given sent my body into what felt like a state of shock. I was shivering uncontrollably, and when the shivering stopped, my body would have to endure contractions. I had to feel the pain of labour, but there was no baby to hold at the end of it.
Nothing could be done to ease my pain, knowing that there was no possibility of a different ending. I was handed a death certificate for someone who never even had a birth certificate.
It is estimated that one in four to six pregnancies ends in miscarriage. But the statistics are complex. There are a multitude of factors that can play a role.
Most of the websites I have visited state that miscarriages are common. And this makes me question: Why is there so little conversation about something that affects women so deeply?
A pregnancy loss is deeply personal, and it should always be a woman’s prerogative to decide whether she wants to talk about it. But for those who do want to talk about it, do we have enough safe spaces?
There is so little mental health support for women going through a loss like this. I was genuinely grateful for the hospital staff who consoled me, who held my hand when my body was going through unbearable pain, and for the doctors who treated me with respect and dignity. But is that guaranteed for every woman who experiences a loss like this?
Too often, these losses are minimised with statements such as, “It was not meant to be.” As though a few words can make the grief disappear. We should hold space for women who are going through these losses and create more meaningful systems of support.
When even “rich” countries struggle to fund research into miscarriage and pregnancy loss, there is little hope for a country like Bangladesh.
The world can be an extremely cruel place for women. But I refuse to be anything but kind to myself.
There was a version of me that existed before the miscarriage, and there is a version of me that exists now. I do not think they are the same person.
The trivial things in life that used to bother me no longer seem to matter. Things I once thought were important have suddenly lost weight. There is something about losing something so deeply wanted that changes your understanding of what truly matters.
While I do not want my pregnancy loss to define me, I also cannot pretend that it is not a part of who I am now. I will carry this loss with me, and I will not allow it to be swept under the carpet or reduced to something that simply happened and should be forgotten.
I am still grieving the future I do not get to have. There is no linear path through a loss this profound. I was applauded for being brave, but the truth is, I was forced to be brave.
I no longer want to be courageous. I want to mourn. I want to grieve the life I never got to meet, on my own terms.
It is the strength of my parents, partner, and siblings that has kept me going. Life keeps moving forward, even though it felt like mine had stopped for a while.
The only lesson I carry forward is that I will show up with love, strength, and support for any woman who has gone through something similar. There should be more conversations about this reality, about a kind of loss that can be so profound and yet have no logical answers. Women should be allowed to grieve without being told how they should grieve.
Ahona Hassan is a human rights activist passionate about speaking on issues often left unspoken.

item.title: A collective failure
Time to deliver to climate promises
UN climate chief urges debt-free climate finance for developing nations
item.description:
UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell has called for a fundamental shift in the global climate finance system, urging developed countries, financial institutions and investors to ensure that funding helps developing nations escape mounting debt pressures and build long-term economic resilience.
Speaking at the Seventh Biennial High-Level Ministerial Dialogue on Climate Finance at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, on Friday, Stiell warned that many developing countries remain trapped in a cycle of debt, climate disasters and increasingly expensive borrowing, leaving them with fewer resources to protect their people and economies.
“Climate finance must help countries break free,” he said, stressing that meeting international funding targets alone would not necessarily address the actual financial needs of vulnerable nations.
He argued that climate finance must move beyond funding individual projects towards supporting broader economic transformation, strengthening national institutions and creating conditions that attract more investment at lower costs.
Under the new climate finance goals agreed at COP29, developed countries are expected to take the lead in providing $300 billion annually by 2035, while all actors are expected to work together to scale up financing for developing countries from all sources to $1.3 trillion per year by the same year.
Stiell said the Baku-to-Belém Roadmap provides a pathway towards achieving these targets, but stressed that the way climate finance is delivered must change to make the commitments meaningful.
Explaining the financial challenges facing developing countries, Stiell said the growing threat of floods, wildfires, storms and droughts increases borrowing costs even before disasters occur.
When climate shocks strike, government revenues decline while recovery and reconstruction expenses rise, pushing countries further into debt.
This leaves governments with fewer resources to invest in climate adaptation, resilience and low-emission development, reinforcing a cycle of financial vulnerability.
To break this cycle, he called for climate finance that reflects individual countries' economic circumstances and debt sustainability.
He emphasised that funding must be affordable and tailored to national needs rather than delivered through a one-size-fits-all approach.
While private finance, loans and guarantees remain important for meeting global climate goals, he said grants and highly concessional financing would continue to be essential, particularly for least developed countries (LDCs), small island developing states (SIDS) and other vulnerable economies.
He also called for broader international efforts to address debt burdens so that developing countries are not forced to choose between repaying loans and investing in climate resilience.
Stiell identified easier access to climate finance as another major priority, pointing to the complicated administrative requirements and fragmented funding arrangements that developing countries must navigate.
He said countries often face complex procedures to access funding from multiple programmes and institutions, making it difficult to secure resources when they are needed.
“We need procedures simplified,” he said, calling for stronger coordination among financial institutions and reduced administrative burdens.
He also stressed that international climate finance should align with national development priorities rather than requiring countries to reshape their domestic systems to meet external funding requirements.
National treasuries, local governments, development banks and financial institutions already play important roles in financing development, and these institutions should be strengthened rather than bypassed, he said.
Stiell urged international partners to invest in institutional capacity and help developing countries establish effective systems to access, manage and deploy climate finance.
He also underscored the importance of developing and transferring technologies that support climate-resilient and low-emission development.
The UN climate chief further called for stronger cooperation among governments, climate funds, development banks, financial institutions and private investors to turn national climate plans into tangible investments.
He said climate finance, technology transfer and capacity-building must work together around countries' own priorities, ensuring that funding translates into projects that strengthen resilience and improve people's lives.
As an example, he explained that early grant-based support could help countries build institutional capacity and develop investment pipelines, while concessional finance and risk-sharing instruments could subsequently help projects expand.
He said international climate negotiations and cooperation mechanisms could play an important role in bringing different sources of finance together around national development priorities.
Concluding his remarks, Stiell called for a new approach to international climate finance, saying the biennial ministerial dialogues should help translate commitments into more effective delivery.
Established in 2013, the dialogues have contributed to discussions on global climate finance. However, he said they must now help advance a system that supports long-term development rather than focusing solely on individual funding targets.
“Where every dollar invested in development builds a better future. For all countries,” he said.
His remarks at COP31 highlight a central challenge for developing countries such as Bangladesh: securing not only greater volumes of climate finance but also affordable, accessible and predictable funding that can strengthen economic resilience without deepening existing debt pressures.

item.title: Dhaka-Chittagong highway: 13km tailback leaves commuters stranded
item.description:
A 13km traffic jam on the Comilla-bound lane of the Dhaka-Chittagong highway caused severe suffering for passengers and drivers on Friday, leaving long-distance buses, trucks and other vehicles stranded for hours.
The congestion began around 7:30am after a covered van broke down on the approach to the Meghna-Gomti Bridge in Daudkandi, disrupting traffic towards Comilla. As the number of vehicles grew, the tailback stretched nearly 13km through the Gazaria section.
Vehicles were moving slowly or stopping intermittently at several points along the highway, according to local residents and police.
Shahabuddin, a bus passenger travelling to his village home, said he regularly faced delays while travelling between Dhaka and his hometown, particularly on holidays and during family occasions. He questioned when a lasting solution to the recurring congestion would come.
Truck driver Sirajul Islam Pintu said it took him one and a half hours to reach Bhaterchar bus stand after getting stuck in traffic near Jamaldi.
Another truck driver, Shakil Mia, said he spent around an hour travelling from Jamaldi to Anarpura bus stand.
Moniruzzaman, in-charge of the Bhaberchar Highway Police Outpost, said the breakdown of the covered van near the bridge had caused the congestion.
Authorities were working to remove the vehicle, and traffic could return to normal within an hour, he said.
Passengers and transport workers have long faced delays on different stretches of the highway, with commuters calling for quicker removal of broken-down vehicles and measures to ensure smoother traffic movement.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,304 as five die in 24 hours
item.description:
Five more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Friday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,304 .
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all five of the latest casualties as suspected .
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,199, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 105, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours .
Among the five new suspected fatalities, the highest concentration was recorded in the Sylhet division with three deaths.
A total of 1,271 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Friday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 245,562 .
During the same period, 148 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 25,028 .
Since March 15, 2026, a total of 219,247 suspected measles patients have been hospitalized across the country, of whom 210,401 have recovered and been discharged from hospitals, according to the DGHS .

item.title: High vegetable, fish and meat prices keep Dhaka consumers under pressure
item.description:
Winter has yet to fully set in in Dhaka, but consumers are already facing high prices for vegetables and other essential food items, with little relief in the markets for fish, meat and eggs.
Vegetable prices usually begin to fall as winter approaches and supplies of seasonal produce increase. However, the expected decline is yet to materialise, leaving consumers struggling to manage their daily expenses.
The situation was observed during visits to several kitchen markets in the capital on Friday.
Vendors said supplies of winter vegetables remained limited as the season had not fully begun. Prices may ease in the coming weeks as more seasonal produce reaches the markets.
A market survey found that new potatoes were selling at Tk140-160 per kg, while old potatoes cost Tk30. Green chillies were priced at Tk120 per kg, round eggplants at Tk100, long eggplants at Tk60-80, bitter gourds at Tk80-100, beans at Tk80-120 depending on variety, cucumbers at Tk100 and carrots at Tk100.
Cauliflowers were selling at Tk50-80 per kg, depending on size. Ridge gourds, pointed gourds, snake gourds, okra and radishes were priced at Tk60 per kg.
Fish prices also remained largely unchanged, with most varieties selling at elevated rates.
Rohu was selling at Tk280-380 per kg, large tilapia at Tk180-200, silver carp and grass carp at Tk180-200, and pangas at Tk160-250.
Katla was priced at Tk350-380 per kg, farmed koi at Tk200-220 and pabda at Tk380-420.
Ilish remained beyond the reach of many consumers, selling at Tk800-2,300 per kg, while larger fish cost more than Tk2,600 per kg.
A dozen brown eggs were selling at Tk145-150, while white eggs cost Tk130-135, adding to consumers' daily expenses.
Meat prices also remained largely unchanged from the previous week. Broiler chicken was selling at Tk170-190 per kg and Sonali chicken at Tk240-330.
Beef was priced at Tk800-850 per kg, while mutton cost Tk1,200-1,250.
Sijan Rahman, a vegetable seller at Dhupkhola market, said supplies of fresh winter vegetables were still limited.
"Prices will fall once new vegetables start arriving in the markets. They may come down somewhat after another week. When several varieties of the same vegetable become available, it is a sign that prices are starting to fall," he said.
Sheikh Nayeem, who was shopping at Sutrapur market, said high prices had made it difficult for ordinary consumers to buy vegetables and fish.
"I cannot afford to buy many vegetables because of their high prices. It will become difficult to run a household if things continue like this," he said.
He added that he eventually left the fish market without buying anything because of the high prices.
"Fish that used to cost Tk800 now cannot be found even for Tk1,200. If the prices of essential commodities continue to rise like this, it will become increasingly difficult for ordinary people to manage their households," he said.

item.title: Bangladesh waits longer for offshore oil, gas exploration
item.description:
Bangladesh may have to wait at least two more years to begin offshore oil and gas exploration, as an extension of the bidding deadline is likely to delay the selection of companies and signing of contracts.
The deadline for submitting bids under the 2026 offshore bidding round has been extended to March 31 next year from November 30 this year. After bids are submitted, evaluation, negotiations and contract finalisation could take until late 2027, according to sources familiar with the process.
Even after contracts are signed, exploration cannot begin immediately. Companies will need to mobilise vessels and equipment and wait for favourable weather conditions at sea.
Experts say offshore exploration is largely weather-dependent. The sea is generally calmer between October and March, making it easier to operate exploration vessels. Rough conditions during the monsoon months, from April to September, make offshore operations difficult.
If the contract process continues until late 2027, companies may miss the next exploration season. In that case, work could be pushed back to the following favourable window, meaning exploration is unlikely to begin before October 2028.
The delay comes as domestic gas production continues to decline and Bangladesh becomes increasingly dependent on imported liquefied natural gas (LNG) to meet demand.
The government extended the bidding deadline following requests from potential investors, who sought more time to prepare their proposals. The issue was discussed during a recent London visit by the state minister for energy, who also chairs the Bangladesh Investment Development Authority (BIDA).
The bidding round, launched on May 24 this year, offers 26 blocks in the Bay of Bengal — 11 in shallow waters and 15 in deep waters. The government has revised several terms, including gas pricing and tax concessions, under a new production sharing contract (PSC) to attract foreign companies.
Turkish Petroleum Overseas Company (TPOC) and China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC) have purchased bidding documents. Several other companies, including Beringia Power Bangladesh, KrisEnergy, Pial Engineering and Construction, Onoda Inc, Rystad Energy and Max Infrastructure, have also purchased data.
A Petrobangla official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the deadline extension was necessary due to limited interest and requests from companies. The official expressed hope that the process would eventually attract bids, despite the delay.
Energy expert BD Rahmat Ullah said Bangladesh was already years behind in offshore exploration and would need at least five to seven years to obtain gas even if exploration began now.
He warned that the latest extension could push the country further behind, while neighbouring Myanmar was reportedly extracting gas from the same maritime region.
Energy expert Shamsul Alam blamed corruption in the energy sector for the delays, alleging that companies had faced demands for shares from people associated with the previous government, discouraging investment.

item.title: Sri Lanka: Rights groups sound alarm over proposed anti-terror law
item.description:
For 46-year-old Ganesan (name changed) from Batticaloa in eastern Sri Lanka, any discussion of terrorism brings back memories of his two-year-old daughter, who was killed in the 2019 Easter Sunday attacks. She was one of 270 people who lost their lives in a series of coordinated bombings targeting three churches and three luxury hotels across the island nation.
The attacks were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. More than 500 people were injured.
Ganesan’s daughter was killed in an attack on the Zion Church in Batticaloa.
But Ganesan remains skeptical when asked about the new counterterrorism bill pushed by the government in Sri Lanka.
“Laws against terrorism are necessary to prevent terrorist attacks, but they should not target the innocent or suppress human rights,” he told DW.
The administration led by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake and his National People’s Power faction
has proposed the Protection of the State from Terrorism Act (Psta) as a replacement for the existing Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). The PTA has many critics who claim that the contentious law has enabled arbitrary detention and the torture of detainees for decades.
The government argues that a robust anti-terrorism law is needed to address the increasingly complex local and international activities of extremist groups.
Rights groups are now also sharply criticizing the new bill. Activist argue that the changes will not bring about any improvement, warning that the draft features an overly broad definition of terrorism, provides inadequate judicial oversight, and grants extensive powers to law enforcement authorities. Activists also warn that the proposed law has only limited safeguards against official abuse.
The bill, for instance, allows security forces to stop, search and question individuals on the basis of “reasonable suspicion,” enter and search premises, and seize items on suspicion of them being linked to an offense under the terrorism act.
“The definition of the term ‘terrorism’ in the bill as presently drafted is highly problematic. The term is unclear, and its meaning has not been clearly defined,” Visakesa Chandrasekaram, a film director and human rights lawyer, told DW.
“Such lack of clarity in the law may result in violations of the fundamental rights of the people,” he added.
Chandrasekaram also pointed out that the bill would confer police powers on the military, which is neither trained to investigate criminal offenses nor equipped to protect the rights of people targeted in such investigations.
This, he warned, could lead to the “militarization” of the law enforcement process.
Dhanushka Silva, a lawyer, said the proposed law is not much different from the existing one.
“The present government pledged to repeal the PTA in their 2024 election manifesto. But now the government seems to replace it with a new act that is a replica of the PTA,” he told DW.
Silva believes the new bill, Psta, could be misused to suppress democratic freedoms and muzzle dissent and free speech.
Under Section 9 of the Psta, even posts or statements made on social media could be subject to scrutiny due to the broad definition of terrorism-related offenses in the bill, he explained.
The section further suggests that individuals who share content deemed to be a terrorism offense could face up to 15 years of rigorous imprisonment, according to the lawyer.
“This is a big blow to freedom of speech in a democratic society like ours,” he said.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (Ohchr) has also called on the government to ensure that the bill is consistent with international human rights law.
It noted that the Psta, despite containing some additional safeguards and improvements on previous drafts, reproduces a number of shortcomings in the PTA and other, older counter-terrorism bills.
The legislation “should include robust safeguards against torture, ill-treatment, enforced disappearance and coercive interrogation,” Ohchr said in a statement.
Government spokesperson Nalinda Jayatissa, however, rejected the allegations by rights activists and insisted that the new law would not compromise civil liberties and press freedom.
Passing the new counterterrorism legislation could also have economic and foreign policy ramifications for Sri Lanka.
The United Nations, which has repeatedly urged Colombo to repeal the PTA, has called for further revisions to the proposed Psta.
The European Union has likewise urged Sri Lanka to uphold its international human rights obligations if it wishes to continue benefiting from the bloc’s Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+), which grants preferential access to the EU market to eligible developing countries.
Failure to meet these requirements could result in the suspension of GSP+ preferences, likely to trigger significant economic penalties for the country.
During a parliamentary debate on November 12, Speaker Jagath Wickramaratne said that some provisions of the proposed law were inconsistent with the constitution.
The legislation was also challenged before the Supreme Court, which outlined several amendments and said Parliament could pass the measure once the changes were made.
Parliament has yet to set a date for a vote.

item.title: Bollywood bolsters security as underworld fears return
item.description:
It sounds like a Bollywood thriller, but a spate of shootings and extortion threats targeting Mumbai’s stars has sent the industry scrambling for bodyguards, reviving memories of the underworld’s grip on cinema in the 1990s.
From gunshots to cash demands, the incidents have unsettled the Indian industry, decades after police crackdowns weakened the criminal gangs once deeply embedded in the multi-billion-dollar business.
Police have linked the latest violence to the gang of Lawrence Bishnoi, a convicted Indian gangster accused by US prosecutors of directing a global criminal network from behind bars.
“Stars are moving around with bodyguards on either side,” actor and security agency owner Ronit Roy said.
“There has been a sharp increase in demand... Requests have expanded beyond just lead actors, to include family members and children.”
Author S. Hussain Zaidi, a former investigative journalist, said opportunistic criminals were exploiting the notoriety of established gangsters.
“Some desperadoes are opening fire in the air to scare the industry and spread fear,” Zaidi told AFP.
“And they have succeeded -- as people have started believing that the mafia-dominated 1990s era is back.”
The latest incidents include gunfire targeting actor Tiger Shroff’s car in Mumbai in October, and an alleged $600,000 extortion demand against actor Tusshar Kapoor.
Police have arrested 13 people under organized crime laws in connection with the October shooting, alleging it was intended to extort money, establish gang dominance and spread fear.
Police said there had also been surveillance of other prominent figures.
They have named Anil Pandit, an alleged Bishnoi gang member, as wanted in connection with the shooting.
Anxiety reverberating across the industry has spilt into public view.
Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan recently greeted fans from behind a bulletproof enclosure outside his Mumbai home during his customary Sunday appearance, while security was beefed up around actor Shah Rukh Khan’s home for his birthday.
But Zaidi said the major gangsters of the 1990s were now dead, imprisoned or inactive.
“The only gangster we hear of these days is Lawrence Bishnoi and even he is in jail, so there is no way that any local Mumbai-based gangster has control over the city,” he said.
The late 1990s and early 2000s were among Bollywood’s darkest periods, when criminal syndicates used threats, extortion and violence to influence film financing, casting and distribution.
They included Dawood Ibrahim, a UN-sanctioned fugitive accused of involvement in the 1993 Mumbai bombings that killed 257 people, and his former lieutenant turned rival Chhota Rajan, who is behind bars in India.
Producers were pressured to pay protection money, surrender business interests and bow to gangsters’ demands.
The underworld’s influence waned as police intensified operations, strengthened by laws passed in 1999 targeting organized crime, while the growth of corporate financing further reduced gangsters’ influence over the film business.
Rajiv Rai, director of the hit thriller “Gupt,” received extortion demands and threatening calls in the late 1990s before eventually leaving India for Britain.
“I was the victim in the 1990s, the world knows,” he told AFP.
Watching the latest incidents unfold, Rai said the motives were harder to decipher.
Bishnoi’s gang has been linked to threats against Salman Khan, reportedly over allegations that the Bollywood star had hunted blackbuck antelopes in 1998.
The animals are revered by the Bishnoi community, a Hindu sect whose faith places strong emphasis on wildlife protection.
Indian authorities have also accused gang members of opening fire outside Khan’s Mumbai home and of involvement in the killing of Baba Siddique, a prominent politician with close ties to the film industry, in 2024.
After the October shooting targeting Shroff, a social media post and audio message attributed to a Bishnoi gang associate reportedly claimed responsibility, citing the actor’s closeness to Khan.
“In the 1990s, we knew their agenda... ransom money,” Rai said.
“Now they are calling and saying if you are Salman’s friend, we will kill you... now what kind of agenda is this?”
Ahmed Ali, a crime journalist, said he believed that “many of these seem to be prank calls, to cash in on the situation that Bishnoi has created.”
Producer Boney Kapoor, who was targeted by underworld figures over a dispute involving overseas distribution rights for his 1997 Salman Khan film “Judwaa,” believes the latest wave of violence will be “short-lived.”
“I don’t feel that kind of fear,” he said. ”But one has to be cautious, these shootings can’t be ignored.”

item.title: Shama calls for predictable, cost-free financing for gender-responsive climate action
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam has called for predictable, accessible and cost-free financing for gender-responsive climate adaptation and resilience.
She made the call while speaking at an event titled “Policy to Practice: Strengthening Gender-responsive Climate Governance and Finance in Bangladesh” at the Bangladesh Pavilion in the Blue Zone of the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Turkiye, on Thursday.
The event was jointly organised by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, and UN Women Bangladesh. Shama attended the event as the chief guest.
The event highlighted Bangladesh’s experiences, emerging lessons, and implementation challenges, with particular attention to institutional capacity, inter-ministerial coordination, sectoral mainstreaming, and gender-responsive climate finance.
It also explored how development partners and international financial institutions could help strengthen the enabling environment and mobilise resources for country-led climate priorities.
In her remarks, the state minister emphasised that safety, mobility, and participation must be integrated into climate adaptation planning from the outset rather than treated as afterthoughts.
She stressed the need for initiatives such as cyclone shelters with separate facilities for women and improved access to reproductive and mental healthcare.
Shama also underscored that gender-responsive climate action should not be limited to one-off projects but must be embedded in the way resilience initiatives are planned, financed, implemented, and monitored.
"When women lead and participate fully, our communities become more resilient, and our future becomes more secure," she said.

Gold, smartphones worth Tk1.13C seized at Dhaka airport
item.description:
The Customs Intelligence and Investigation Directorate (CIID) seized gold bars weighing 471 grams, 35 smartphones and other goods worth around Tk 1.13 crore in three separate drives at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport on Thursday.
The seizures were made during the operations conducted by the CIID’s A-shift team, following increased vigilance against smuggling and customs duty evasion through passenger baggage, according to a press release issued on Friday.
In one operation, 171 grams of gold bars, along with cosmetics, food items and medicines, were recovered from the baggage of passenger Md Abul Hossain, who arrived in Dhaka from Bangkok on a US-Bangla Airlines flight.
The seized goods were estimated to be worth Tk 35.70 lakh.
In another drive, customs officials recovered 300 grams of gold bars, 35 smartphones of Samsung, Honor and Realme brands, 36 kg of soap and 6.375 kg of cosmetics from the baggage of passenger Shah Alam Aziz.
He arrived from Bangkok on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight.
After allowing 100 grams of gold under passenger baggage facilities, subject to payment of applicable duties and taxes and the required passport endorsement, officials seized the remaining excess gold and other goods.
The seized items were valued at around Tk 55.30 lakh.
In a separate search of the baggage of another passenger, Umma Hani, arriving on the same Biman flight, officials found 200 grams of gold bars and 40.48 kg of soap.
After allowing 100 grams of gold under baggage facilities, the customs officials seized the remaining gold and excess goods, valued at approximately Tk 21.77 lakh.
The CIID said the increasing number of attempts to bring gold and smartphones in small consignments pointed to an emerging smuggling risk at the airport.
Although individual consignments may appear relatively small, their cumulative impact could result in substantial revenue losses, it said.
The directorate is also examining whether such incidents are linked to organised smuggling networks.
The CIID said it had strengthened intelligence surveillance and intensified operations to counter changing smuggling methods and protect government revenue.
