BB eases LC conditions for 11 essential commodities ahead of Ramadan
item.description:
Bangladesh Bank has relaxed conditions for opening Letters of Credit (LCs) for imports to ensure a smooth supply of essential commodities during the upcoming month of Ramadan.
From now on, commercial banks can determine the cash margin rate for opening LCs for designated goods based on their bank-customer relationships.
On Sunday (November 8), the Banking Regulations and Policy Department-1 of Bangladesh Bank issued a circular regarding this matter.
The directive has been sent to the managing directors and chief executive officers of all scheduled banks in the country.
The circular stated that the demand for essential daily items increases during Ramadan.
This initiative aims to facilitate imports, maintain a steady supply of goods in the market, and keep prices at a tolerable level during this period.
According to the guidelines, the cash margin for opening LCs for importing rice, wheat, onions, pulses, soybean and palm oil, sugar, chickpeas, yellow peas, spices, and dates can be settled on the basis of bank-customer relationships.
Additionally, the central bank advised commercial banks to prioritize importers when opening LCs to ensure an adequate supply of these commodities in the domestic market.
Bangladesh Bank noted that this directive was issued in the public interest using powers conferred under Section 45 of the Bank Company Act, 1991.
The order takes effect immediately and will remain in force until March 15, 2027.

item.title: Khasru: Found discrepancies in previous govt’s GDP calculations
item.description:
Massive discrepancies and inconsistencies have been identified in the calculation of the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) during the previous government's tenure.
The government announced that these anomalies were uncovered through a forensic audit, and the report will be made public shortly following expert review.
Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury and Minister of State for Planning Md. Jonayed Abdur Rahim Saki shared this information Sunday at a discussion meeting held at the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) auditorium in the capital, on the occasion of National Statistics Day.
At the same time, the government announced that full independence is being granted to the Bureau of Statistics (BBS) to restore the neutrality of data and public trust in statistics.
Speaking as the chief guest, Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khasru Mahmud Chowdhury emphasized data transparency, stating that work cannot be carried out using questionable statistics as it is akin to deceiving oneself.
Pointing out that data is the government's most critical asset, he affirmed that BBS is being given complete independence.
Clarifying the review of past calculations, the minister stressed that the audit's purpose is not to target anyone personally. He noted that the forensic audit was conducted to delve into past irregularities, not to target individuals, adding that the more data is made open, the more errors and inconsistencies will surface, creating opportunities for correction.
The minister also mentioned that alongside addressing manpower shortages, the government is prioritizing digital infrastructure and the use of artificial intelligence in this tech era.
Adviser to the Ministry of Finance and Planning, Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, stated that during the previous government's tenure, statistics were weaponized to construct a specific political narrative.
Highlighting significant discrepancies in the list of social safety net beneficiaries alongside GDP data, the minister noted that many of those who genuinely deserved assistance were deprived.
Citing a concrete example of statistical discrepancy, the minister shared that the number of registered vessels in the country was previously shown as a mere 13,000, whereas a recent review revealed the actual number to be 267,000.
He announced that initiatives are underway to establish an integrated "Digital Register" system soon to eliminate such anomalies.
Speaking as a special guest, Minister of State for Planning Md. Jonayed Abdur Rahim Saki stated that without accurate data, it is impossible to understand where the country stands, where it intends to go, or where mistakes are occurring. Hence, initiatives have been launched to rebuild the public's lost faith in statistics.
The State Minister added that effective measures have already been taken to reduce government interference in data. As part of these measures, the BBS now directly releases all crucial economic metrics, including the Consumer Price Index (CPI), without requiring prior approval or signatures from any minister.
Chaired by Md Firoz Sarkar, secretary of the Statistics and Informatics Division, the event opened with welcome remarks by BBS Director General Md Shamimul Huq.
Additionally, Prime Minister's Political Adviser Zahir Uddin Swapan, Dhaka University Professor Syed Shahadat Hossain, and Director General of the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies (BIDS) AK Enamul Haque also addressed the meeting.

item.title: HSBC commits $1bn for disaster preparedness in Bangladesh
item.description:
HSBC announced details of its disaster preparedness partnership in Bangladesh with Unicef, the British Red Cross and Save the Children, to support communities prepare for emergencies and enable HSBC funding to reach them faster when crises strike.
The activity forms part of HSBC’s Disaster Relief Partnership, backed by a commitment of $4.5 million over an initial 18-month pilot period, supporting projects in countries including Bangladesh, Vietnam, Kenya and the Philippines.
Launched globally on October 13, 2026, the partnership combines HSBC funding with the expertise and reach of three leading humanitarian organizations.
In Bangladesh, approximately $1 million has so far been allocated to support three specific disaster preparedness projects.
The projects will work to strengthen community preparedness and resilience, supporting early action ahead of predicted emergencies such as flooding or landslides, in helping to protect lives and livelihoods.
The “HSBC’s Disaster Relief Partnership - Launch in Bangladesh,” ceremony took place in Dhaka recently and was attended by Surendra Rosha, co-chief executive of Asia and Middle East, HSBC; Md Mahbub ur Rahman, chief executive officer of HSBC Bangladesh; Antonio Granco Garcia, chief of field service, Unicef Bangladesh; Mukesh Kumar Singh, country representative, the British Red Cross; Rahmat Ullah Bhuiyan, deputy country director, Save the Children; James Goldman, deputy high commissioner and development director to Bangladesh, British High Commission.
Surendra Rosha, co-chief executive of Asia and Middle East, HSBC said: “Long-term economic growth across our international markets depends directly on community resilience. By bringing together HSBC’s global reach and the frontline expertise of our humanitarian partners, we are helping vulnerable regions across Asia shift from simply reacting to crises to preparing for them before they happen.”
Commenting on the country launch, Md Mahbub ur Rahman, chief executive officer, HSBC Bangladesh said: “Economic resilience in Bangladesh starts with local preparedness. Through this collaboration with Unicef, the Red Cross, and Save the Children, we are putting resources where they matter most which is building long-term defenses so vulnerable communities can anticipate and withstand climate challenges.”
Antonio Franco García, chief field services of Unicef in Bangladesh said: “For children in Bangladesh, floods, cyclones and disease outbreaks can quickly become life-threatening emergencies. Investing in preparedness means acting before disaster strikes, not only responding afterwards. Through this partnership with HSBC, we will help vulnerable communities anticipate risks, act early and better protect children, building a safer and more resilient future for every child.”
Mukesh Singh, country representative, the British Red Cross, said: “Lasting change happens when communities have the power, resources, and support to act. Through HSBC’s partnership, the British Red Cross together with the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society can strengthen locally led preparedness, response, and climate action, enabling communities to better anticipate, adapt to, and recover from crises.”
ASM Rahmat Ullah, deputy country director, Save the Children said: “We acknowledge the support from HSBC which has strengthened Save the Children’s organizational systems for localized risk monitoring and anticipatory action while enabling timely, targeted support to the most vulnerable households ahead of an emergency, empowering communities to act early, build local resilience and minimize disaster impacts.”
This unique collaboration offers an important opportunity to learn and share best practices.
The partnership also aims to strengthen the collective ability of partners to provide HSBC support at pace, build resilience and support disaster mitigation efforts.

item.title: PM mourns death of 7 Bangladeshis in Saudi road accident
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Sunday expressed deep shock and sorrow over the death of seven Bangladeshi nationals in a road accident in Saudi Arabia.
The premier, in a condolence message this morning, said: "I express my deep shock and sorrow over the death of seven Bangladeshi nationals and injuries to six others in a tragic road accident in Saudi Arabia on November 7."
He also extended heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families, prayed for the eternal peace of the departed souls and wished the injured a speedy and full recovery, said PM's Press Secretary AAM Saleh Shibli.
"In this difficult time, the government of Bangladesh stands by the affected families," he said, adding that "The Bangladesh Embassy and Consulate in Saudi Arabia will continue to provide all necessary assistance to the families of the victims and the injured."

item.title: Savar-Ashulia industrial activity normalises, 20 factories shut
item.description:
Industrial activity has largely returned to normal in Savar and Ashulia following several days of unrest over garment workers’ demands, including a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000 and an end to blacklisting.
Most factories resumed production on Sunday, although authorities declared holidays at 20 factories after workers at several facilities stopped working and remained inside their workplaces.
After the holiday announcements around 10:30am, workers from several factories took positions on the Abdullahpur-Baipail road. Police later persuaded them to leave the road. Speaking around noon, Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of police of Ashulia Industrial Police-1, said workers were carrying out their duties peacefully at most factories in Savar and Ashulia.
However, workers at several factories had stopped working and remained inside, prompting the authorities to declare holidays at 20 factories. Workers at four factories were still refusing to work, he added.
He said some workers took to the streets, but police persuaded them to move away.
The Savar Upazila administration said 11 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), along with police personnel, had been deployed to maintain law and order, keep factories operational and ensure uninterrupted production.
Speaking around 12:45pm, Khairul Mamun, legal affairs secretary of the Bangladesh Garments and Sweaters Workers Trade Union Centre, said workers at several factories had returned to work.
However, authorities had declared holidays at some factories after workers stopped working and remained inside, while workers at a few others were still refusing to work.
Overall, the situation was satisfactory for the time being, he said, stressing that ensuring workers receive their wages by the 10th of the month should now be the top priority.
Savar Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Md Saiful Islam said the situation in the industrial areas of Savar was currently normal, with workers returning to their workplaces.
However, the period leading up to the 10th of the month would be crucial for wage payments, and the administration was closely monitoring the situation, he said.
Factory owners had been instructed to pay workers within the stipulated deadline.
The UNO added that 11 platoons of BGB, nine executive magistrates and members of various law enforcement agencies had been deployed to maintain normalcy in the area.

item.title: Defiant Khawaja defends re-igniting ball-tampering scandal
item.description:
Usman Khawaja insisted Sunday he did not "throw anyone under the bus" by claiming the entire Australian team was in on the 2018 "Sandpapergate" plot and defended taking eight years to go public.
The retired batsman re-ignited the infamous ball-tampering scandal in Cape Town on Saturday ahead of the release of his autobiography this week, where a chapter is dedicated to the issue.
He alleged that it was not just Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft -- who were all subsequently banned -- who were responsible.
"It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," he said.
Khawaja claimed Australia also employed the tactic during the previous Test at Port Elizabeth.
In response Darren Lehmann, who was head coach at the time, denied there was widespread knowledge of the plot while Cricket Australia said it was "comfortable" with the findings of its original investigation.
That probe found only Smith, Warner and Bancroft were in the know.
"When I mentioned it was all of us, that's implying that whether we like it or not, we're all responsible for what happened together as a team," Khawaja said in a lengthy Instagram post on Sunday.
"We need to take that collectively. That is all."
He added: "I haven't thrown anyone under the bus.
"The guys that are currently in the team right now and the other people that were there on the South African tour, including me, we're not the victims.
"These three guys (Smith, Warner and Bancroft) took the blame for all of us.
"They're the victims ... people telling them that they're cheats, getting nailed by the crowd. Public humiliation."
Khawaja, who retired this year after 88 Tests, defended waiting so long to make the claims, denying it was a marketing ploy to sell his book.
He said he wanted to go public in 2018 once Smith, Warner and Bancroft were suspended.
"But Smudge (Smith) being the man and leader he was, he talked me out of it.
"He wanted to take the blame. I argued with him, but he was having none of it. That's the first time I tried to come out."
Khawaja said he again almost spoke up in 2021 when bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all denied publicly that they knew about the ball-tampering.
But after extensive talks with then-coach Justin Langer he decided not to.
The 39-year-old said he never felt comfortable talking after that while back in the Australian team from 2022.
"Call me a chicken or whatever you want. I didn't know how to do it because I was still in the team," Khawaja said. "I was always conscious of putting my team first, but I'm not in that team anymore."

item.description:
Police recovered the body of a local Jubo Dal leader from a mountain stream in Bandarban town on Sunday morning.

His bloodied body was found in a stream in the Kasaipara area of the district town.
According to police and local residents, people heading to work on Sunday morning spotted a man lying in the stream with blood on his body. His nose and mouth were bleeding. They informed the police, who arrived at the scene, recovered the body and took it to Bandarban Sadar Hospital.
Locals suspect that Sharif may have slipped and fallen into the stream while descending towards it, resulting in his death.
Bandarban Superintendent of Police Md Wahabul Islam Khandaker said police had recovered the body from the stream. The exact cause of death would be determined after an autopsy.

item.title: A day of rallies, tributes and fanfare as BNP makes November 7 historic again
item.description:
The Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) observed National Revolution and Solidarity Day with rallies and programs across the country on Saturday, marking the occasion for the first time with state-level celebrations since returning to power.
The BNP-led government declared November 7 a public holiday and organised official programs to commemorate the historic events of 1975.
In Dhaka, Prime Minister and BNP Chairman Tarique Rahman led a nearly six-kilometre procession from Nayapaltan to Manik Mia Avenue, marking the 51st anniversary of the day.
Photo: Ahadul Karim Khan/Dhaka Tribune
The procession, titled “National Revolution and Solidarity Day Sovereignty Rally”, began around 3:30pm from in front of the BNP's central office after a brief speech by Tarique. It reached Manik Mia Avenue around an hour later, passing through several major roads in the capital.
Thousands of BNP leaders, activists and supporters gathered in Nayapaltan from noon. Leaders of the party's associate and affiliated organisations also joined the procession.
The entire Paltan area turned festive with the presence of leaders and activists of the BNP and its associate and affiliated organisations including Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal, Krishak Dal and Swechchhasebak Dal.
It was Tarique's first participation in a BNP rally since returning to Bangladesh and his first such appearance as the party's chairman.
Earlier in the morning, he paid tribute to BNP founder and former president Ziaur Rahman and former prime minister Khaleda Zia, placing wreaths at their graves at Zia Udyan in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar around 8:30am.
Photo: PMO
The Armed Forces organised special programs, including a display involving 3,000 cadets of the Bangladesh National Cadet Corps and 500 members of Bangladesh Scouts. The Army chief, Air chief, cabinet members, lawmakers, senior government officials and foreign diplomats attended the event.
Various agencies under the home ministry, including Bangladesh Police, Border Guard Bangladesh, Ansar and VDP, the Department of Narcotics Control, Coast Guard, Prisons Directorate and Fire Service and Civil Defence, also arranged milad mahfils, feasts and special darbars.
The BNP is observing the occasion through a seven-day program from November 5 to 11. Alongside the central rally in Dhaka, rallies were held at district and metropolitan levels on Saturday, with further programmes planned at thana and upazila levels on Sunday.
The government also arranged special meals for inmates and residents of hospitals, prisons, orphanages and other state-run institutions. Children were allowed free entry to parks managed by city corporations and municipalities, while educational institutions held discussions and essay competitions.
The Dhaka Elevated Expressway also remained toll-free for all vehicles from 6am to noon on Saturday as part of the observance.

item.title: Dhaka plans two monorail routes by 2030
item.description:
The government is moving ahead with plans to build two monorail routes in Dhaka by 2030, with detailed design work underway following the completion of a pre-feasibility study.
Dhaka Transport Co-ordination Authority (DTCA) Additional Executive Director Dr Md Moshiur Rahman said the proposed monorail system would expand the capital’s public transport network by providing an environmentally friendly, sustainable and efficient transport option, particularly in areas with high passenger demand, reports BSS.
He said the proposed routes could be connected to existing and planned metro rail lines and other public transport services, making it easier for commuters to reach their final destinations from metro stations.
Consultants from the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) have already completed the pre-feasibility study. The detailed designs are now being prepared and are expected to be submitted within six months, according to the project timeline.
The final two routes will be selected based on technical, economic and environmental assessments, taking into account passenger demand, potential benefits and financial viability.
Moshiur said the DTCA conducted transport modelling surveys in different parts of the capital to assess passenger demand and shared the findings with BUET consultants for analysis.
BUET's Bureau of Research, Testing and Consultation (BRTC) completed the pre-feasibility study. Under the agreement, the detailed designs are scheduled to be submitted within the next six months.
The government has allocated Tk7.57 crore from the revenue budget for the pre-feasibility study and detailed designs of the proposed two routes.
The revised Strategic Transport Plan proposes five monorail routes spanning around 79.4km. Authorities plan to select a priority route within three months and complete the overall study within six months.
The five preliminary routes were identified by considering areas where access to feeder bus services for mass rapid transit (MRT) lines is limited.
They are: Airport-Bashundhara via Purbachal and Jolshiri (25.2km); Moddho Badda-Bhulta (14.6km); Rampura-Demra (10.3km); Mohammadpur-Postogola (11.7km); and Airport-Savar via Uttara Centre (17.6km).
The proposal also mentions Monorail-8, from TSC at Dhaka University to Kamrangirchar, with nine stations; Monorail-10, from Alubdi to either West Agargaon or Shyamoli, with 10 stations; and Monorail-13, from Paltan to either Sadarghat or Jhilmil, with six or 11 stations.
A BUET consultant told BSS that the pre-feasibility study examined population patterns, potential passenger catchment areas around stations, gaps in public transport services, traffic congestion, land availability for depots and opportunities for future expansion.
The government-funded assessment will also examine proposed route alignments, potential station and depot locations, passenger demand, technical and structural suitability, economic feasibility, and environmental and social impacts.
A monorail runs on an elevated structure, making it a potential option for densely populated areas where road space is limited and conventional transport infrastructure may be difficult to build.
The study will assess construction and operating costs, passenger capacity and the overall economic and social justification for the proposed system. Local and expatriate Bangladeshi experts have been engaged as consultants.
The initiative is part of the government's broader efforts to ease traffic congestion and improve urban transport in the capital, in line with its election pledges.

item.title: Kurigram municipal worker killed in front of wife at Nov 7 event
item.description:
A municipal worker was stabbed to death with surgical scissors in front of his wife at Kurigram municipal town hall on Saturday afternoon, shortly after the first session of a programme marking National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
The incident took place at the town hall near College Mor in Kurigram Sadar. The victim’s wife was also injured in the attack and later referred to Rangpur Medical College Hospital for advanced treatment.
The deceased, identified as Mansur, 58, had worked for Kurigram Municipality on a daily-wage basis for years and was serving as the town hall caretaker.
According to officials present at the venue, the suspect, identified as Shahnewaz Sani, 32, entered the town hall after the first session of the programme had ended. Mansur told him that the event was over and there was no need to enter the premises, triggering an argument between the two.
At the time, Mansur’s wife, Mallika, 48, arrived with his lunch. As he was taking the food container from her, the suspect allegedly attacked him repeatedly in the chest with a pair of surgical scissors. When Mallika tried to intervene, she was also attacked.
Other employees rushed to help after hearing their screams and took the injured couple to Kurigram General Hospital, where doctors declared Mansur dead.
Local residents detained the suspect and handed him over to police.
Kurigram Sadar Police Station Officer-in-Charge Kamal Hossain said police had recovered the scissors allegedly used in the attack from the suspect.
The victim’s daughter was preparing to file a case, he said, adding that investigators were examining the motive and why the suspect was carrying the scissors.
“The incident initially appears to have been sudden rather than premeditated,” the OC said.
Deputy Commissioner Annapurna Debnath and officials from the police and municipal administration visited the scene after the incident.
Despite the killing, the second session of the National Revolution and Solidarity Day programme continued at the town hall on Saturday evening.

item.title: Minu urges unity in the spirit of National Revolution and Solidarity Day
item.description:
Land Minister Mizanur Rahman Minu on Saturday called upon people from all walks of life to work together in unity to protect national interests, thwart conspiracies, and advance the country towards prosperity.
He made the call while speaking at a discussion meeting held at the auditorium of Rajshahi District Shilpakala Academy, marking National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
The minister said the people of the country had always demonstrated unity in defending their freedom and sovereignty, from the Liberation War to the recent movement against fascism.
Recalling the Liberation War of 1971, Minu paid tributes to the sacrifices of the East Bengal Regiment and valiant freedom fighters in the Battle of Hili and other frontline battles.
Highlighting the significance of November 7, 1975, he said Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman took responsibility for the country during a critical period, enjoying the trust and support of the common people.
He said Ziaur Rahman inspired farmers, introduced banking facilities for young entrepreneurs, and opened new opportunities for economic emancipation through the introduction of the back-to-back letter of credit system in the readymade garment sector.
The minister also recalled Ziaur Rahman's contributions to enhancing Bangladesh's international dignity, including the planting of neem trees, known as 'Zia Trees', at the Arafat field in Saudi Arabia on behalf of the country.
He paid tributes to Ziaur Rahman's simple lifestyle and former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia's sacrifices in establishing democracy.
Referring to the development of Rajshahi, Minu said the establishment of Rajshahi Metropolitan Police (RMP) had laid the foundation for improving law and order in the region, which had since made significant progress.
He further said Rajshahi had emerged as one of the best medium-sized cities in Southeast Asia, developing into a green, clean and healthy city through the collective efforts of its residents.
Expressing optimism about the city's future, he called for continued unity and collective efforts to sustain the positive trend and take Rajshahi further forward.
Later, the minister distributed prizes among the winners of a painting competition organized to mark National Revolution and Solidarity Day.

item.title: Minister: Nation must be built on the ideals of Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman
item.description:
Agriculture, Fisheries and Livestock Minister Mohammed Aminur Rashid on Saturday called upon BNP leaders and activists at all levels to work in unity, inspired by the ideals and patriotism of Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman.
He said one of the key lessons of "National Revolution and Solidarity Day" is the establishment of national unity.
Embracing this spirit, he said, all should work together under the leadership of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman aiming to make the nation stronger and more prosperous one.
The agriculture minister made the remarks while speaking as the chief guest at a discussion meeting, organised by Comilla South District and City units of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), marking the National Revolution and Solidarity Day.
He said November 7 holds great significance in the history of Bangladesh. Amid various political crises and uncertainties, the uprising of soldiers and the public on this day in 1975 carved a unique place for itself in the nation's history, he said.
Aminur said the core essence of this day is to set aside differences and unite, and this unity must be further strengthened in the national interest.
Speakers at the discussion said the National Revolution and Solidarity Day represents a crucial chapter in the country's political history.
They stressed conveying the significance of this day to the younger generation to uphold the ideals of independence, sovereignty, democracy and national unity.

item.title: Police come under attack during AL procession in Chittagong
item.description:
Police came under attack during a procession by the activities-banned Awami League in the Bandar area of Chittagong city on Friday, with 20 people arrested in connection with the incident.
Six police personnel, including Bandar police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Abdur Rahim, were injured in the incident, which took place around 3pm in the Taltala area of Port Connecting Road under Bandar police station.
According to police and local sources, leaders and activists of the activities-banned Awami League brought out a procession in the area on Friday afternoon. After receiving information about the procession, a police team went to the scene and attempted to stop it.
At that point, participants allegedly threw brickbats at police and smashed the glass of a police vehicle, injuring 6 police personnel, including the OC.
Police later chased the procession participants and arrested 20 people from the scene.
A case has been filed with Bandar police station over the attack on police under the Anti-Terrorism Act.
OC Abdur Rahim said brickbats were thrown at police during the procession and the glass of a police vehicle was smashed. He added that police operations to arrest the other participants were continuing.

item.title: The pink bus experience: A smoother ride, if you can catch it
Five priorities for Bangladesh ahead of COP31
item.description:
For decades, Bangladesh has stood at the frontline of climate change. Rising sea levels, cyclones, floods, salinity intrusion, and heat stress have made the country one of the most climate-vulnerable nations in the world.
Yet Bangladesh has also become one of the world's most remarkable examples of climate adaptation and resilience-building.
Discussions on Bangladesh’s climate priorities ahead of COP31 took place during the 64th meeting of the Subsidiary Bodies (SB64) of the UNFCCC in Bonn from June 8-18. The Bangladesh delegation was led by the special assistant to the prime minister of the newly formed government. As in previous years, I had the opportunity to follow the climate discussions and negotiations at SB64 and engage in a dialogue with the special assistant on Bangladesh’s future climate strategies.
Our exchange highlighted an important opportunity: Moving beyond the narrative of vulnerability and positioning Bangladesh as a global leader in climate solutions.
Bangladesh’s experience, particularly in community-led adaptation and resilience-building, offers valuable lessons for the world. At the same time, the country has an opportunity to further strengthen its role in global climate action by combining adaptation leadership with innovation, collaboration, and strategic engagement.
Based on discussions and reflections from SB64, five priorities deserve particular attention as Bangladesh prepares for COP31.
Bangladesh's greatest climate success story is not found in international conference halls but in local communities.
Over the last decades, investments in cyclone preparedness, community-based disaster management, early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, and local adaptation initiatives have dramatically reduced climate-related mortality and strengthened resilience across vulnerable regions.
These achievements are increasingly recognized internationally as examples of successful adaptation in practice.
However, Bangladesh has not always been effective in translating these experiences into global influence. Stronger documentation, monitoring, and communication of adaptation outcomes are needed.
Robust data demonstrating how local adaptation initiatives reduce vulnerability, improve livelihoods, and strengthen resilience can help position Bangladesh as a global knowledge leader.
At a time when many countries are struggling to operationalize adaptation goals, Bangladesh possesses evidence and experience that the world urgently needs.
Adaptation will rightly remain Bangladesh's highest climate priority. Yet adaptation and mitigation should not be viewed as competing agendas.
The most successful climate investments increasingly deliver both emissions reductions and resilience benefits. Renewable energy systems can strengthen energy security during climate-related disruptions. Nature-based solutions such as mangrove restoration can simultaneously store carbon, reduce disaster risks, and protect livelihoods. Climate-smart agriculture can improve food security while reducing emissions.
By prioritizing mitigation projects that generate adaptation co-benefits, Bangladesh can strengthen its international position, attract additional financing, and demonstrate how developing countries can pursue integrated climate action.
Rather than choosing between adaptation and mitigation, Bangladesh can show how the two agendas reinforce one another.
Climate action is most effective when it is co-created. Bangladesh has a vibrant ecosystem of NGOs, community organizations, researchers, youth groups, social enterprises, and local governments working on climate issues. Yet these actors are not always fully integrated into national climate planning and implementation processes.
Future climate strategies should place greater emphasis on collaborative governance, participatory planning, and co-development. Citizens and local communities possess valuable knowledge about risks, vulnerabilities, and practical solutions. Their involvement improves both legitimacy and effectiveness.
International experience increasingly shows that climate transitions succeed when governments act not only as regulators but also as facilitators of collaboration between public, private, academic, and civil society actors.
As climate negotiations become increasingly complex, effective participation requires a diverse range of expertise.
Bangladesh has long been respected within the UNFCCC process, particularly on adaptation and climate justice. However, future negotiations will increasingly involve highly technical discussions around climate finance, carbon markets, technology transfer, loss and damage mechanisms, and implementation frameworks.
To maximize influence at COP31 and beyond, Bangladesh should continue expanding the diversity of expertise within its delegations. Alongside government officials, delegations can benefit from economists, scientists, legal experts, finance specialists, communication professionals, and experienced negotiators.
Strong climate diplomacy requires both technical knowledge and strategic negotiation skills.
Prepare for emerging carbon market opportunities
The operationalization of Article 6 of the Paris Agreement is creating new opportunities for international carbon trading and climate finance.
Many developing countries are now positioning themselves to benefit from emerging carbon markets through high-quality mitigation projects, nature-based solutions, and capacity-building initiatives. Bangladesh should actively prepare for this evolving landscape.
This requires investments in institutional capacity, transparent governance systems, project development expertise, monitoring frameworks, and stakeholder engagement. Universities, research institutions, private sector actors, and local communities all have important roles to play.
If approached strategically, carbon markets could become an additional source of climate finance while supporting sustainable development objectives.
A new chapter
Bangladesh has already demonstrated that climate vulnerability does not prevent climate leadership. The country's achievements in adaptation, disaster risk reduction, and resilience-building are recognized around the world.
The challenge now is to build on that foundation.
By showcasing community-led adaptation successes, integrating mitigation and resilience objectives, strengthening collaborative governance, enhancing negotiation capacity, and preparing for emerging climate finance opportunities, Bangladesh can help shape the global climate agenda rather than simply respond to it.
As the world prepares for COP31, Bangladesh has an opportunity to present itself not only as a country at risk from climate change, but as a country helping to define the solutions.
Dr Avit Bhowmik is a Climate Scientist and Associate Professor of Risk and Environmental Studies, Karlstad University, Sweden.

item.title: Barman, Koch families allegedly left out of govt ethnic minority survey despite gazette recognition
Men neither see nor listen to women
item.description:
Searching the Dhaka Tribune last week for a piece of my own, I came instead upon an essay I have not been able to put down: Shuchi binte Shahjalal’s The women are divine .
She opens with the old belief of the idol-makers: That a Durga is incomplete unless a little earth from a sex worker’s doorstep is worked into her clay -- for a man leaves his virtue at that threshold, and the ground there turns holy. The goddess cannot be finished without the woman’s soil; the woman herself cannot be let into the festival. The earth is holy, she writes. The person is not.
Let me say at once what I am and am not doing. I am a man, and this is a piece about men. I will not presume to explain to the women of my homeland a cage they have mapped, from the inside, far better than I can.
Shuchi has already said the essential thing, with a scholar’s range and a poet’s aim. I want only to add a footnote -- from the poet we Bengalis reach for whenever we wish to sound reverent about women, and whom, I have come to think, we never actually heard.
We are fond of Tagore as a worshipper of the feminine. We quote him at weddings and drape our daughters’ recitals in his songs. It is worth remembering, then, that at his most attentive, the Bishwakobi was not building the pedestal Shuchi describes. He was warning against it.
I have spent this autumn translating his love songs, one line at a time, and two of them will not now leave me.
The first is Bhalobeshe, sokhi, nibhrite jatone -- “Love me, and in the quiet shrine of your heart, write my name.” Midway, the lover makes a stranger, smaller request:
“Keep, with tender care, my chattering bird, in the courtyard of your palace.”
Read it slowly, and the bird is no ornament. The whole ache of the song is the plea that it be kept, tended, listened to.
In a second song, Tumi ki keboli chhobi -- “Are you only a picture?” -- he almost begs her not to harden into mere paint on a canvas, to be real and present, not an image he can hang on a wall and admire.
A century before our present arguments, Tagore had already named the two ways a man fails a woman: He stops listening to her voice, and he lets her freeze into an image.
Shuchi calls on Nazrul, who dared to address the barangana , the prostitute, as “mother,” and asked who had the right to spit at her.
Let me call on the other giant, who stands, I think, exactly where she does -- on the side of the woman no one will look at or listen to.
Her essay is unsparing about what reverence costs, in life and in death. She recalls the roughly 1,500 women driven from the Kandapara brothel in Tangail in 2014, long after a High Court had ruled such evictions unconstitutional; the sex workers ridiculed when they report rape, because the society “cannot imagine a sex worker being raped”; and Hamida Begum, who in 2020 became the first sex worker in Daulatdia to receive a proper Islamic burial -- after which the imam who prayed over her said he would not do it again, having been scolded by his neighbours.
Beside these, she sets the national figures she cites: By the counts of the Bangladesh Mahila Parishad and Ain o Salish Kendra, 786 women and girls raped in 2025, up from 516 the year before; and almost 22,000 cases of violence against women and children logged by police in a single year.
I will not borrow her numbers to decorate an argument of my own. I note only what she notices -- that behind each is a woman whom a society that sorts its women into goddesses and fallen women has filed under the second heading.
And I would underline, for every man who thinks himself devout, the sentence of hers that ought to be read aloud from pulpits: A society that calls its women mothers and then cannot bury them, cannot hear them, and makes the raped one hide her face while the rapist walks, has not forgotten reverence -- it has made reverence a way to keep women in their place.
Here, let me add the one thing a lifetime in medicine has taught me, because it bears on her point that rape is treated as a stain on a woman’s honour rather than a crime against her body.
I have spent my working life with the human heart -- the actual muscle, four chambers, no holier in a saint than in a so-called fallen woman. A body keeps no ledger of honour. It bleeds the same, grieves the same, heals or fails to heal the same, whatever box the neighbours have assigned its owner.
When we treat a woman’s injury as a stain on her family’s ijjat rather than harm to her person, we are not being moral. We are staring at the honour and refusing to see the woman -- the same failure, once more.
So the answer, I think, is not less reverence but reverence that finally opens its eyes. Read generously, the idol-maker’s belief is almost holy: The goddess is made, in part, of the outcast woman’s earth; the divine and the discarded are the same clay.
The tragedy is only that we stop at the clay. We bow to the figure and walk past the person who gave it her soil.
Tagore points where Shuchi points. Keep the chattering bird -- do not cage it, do not silence it, bend down and listen. Do not let her become only a picture on the wall.
The cure for a goddess no one can bear to meet is not to break her into a “fallen” woman; it is to come down off our own certainty and stand beside her at the doorstep -- to see her face, and to hear her voice.
Shuchi binte Shahjalal has written the diagnosis. The least her countrymen -- and I mean the men -- can do is read it with our eyes open for once, and admit what it took a woman on the Op-Ed desk to say plainly.
The idols are immersed. But the women are still at their doorsteps, many still hiding their faces: Divine in theory, and in practice neither seen nor heard.
Rajani K Saha writes from Stockholm, where he practises medicine.
